title: How can i make a game/app multiplayer?
author: PANC0NE
selftext:
As the title says, i've made an app but now the biggest problem is that i do not know how can i make the multiplayer part. 

what do i need to allow people to connect in a session?

comments.author: JaironKalach
comments.body: You need either peer to peer or server based networking code to transport game state changes back and forth to keep the game clients synchronized at the minimum. You need protections to make sure those changes are authoritative and not someone hacking. Since you’re using AI, anyway, I’d recommend using your chat client to go into a deep dive of multiplayer architectures.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
Generally speaking, you need a multiplayer backend somewhere that people can connect to. The normal baseline is to have a domain name (or a subdomain) and pay for a VPS to run a server at that address. If you have a web game, you’d use websockets. Expect to pay some amount of money for hosting ($5/month gives you plenty of options, if you know what you’re doing). It’s technically possible to run games from free hosting options but I wouldn’t bother.

The bad news is that it is hard to make a multiplayer game and you’ll run into a lot of problems along the way.

comments.author: Optimal-Estimate6576
comments.body: If you can’t do this even with the help of AI, I doubt you’ll ever be able to. Instead of asking that question here why don't you ask the same question to your AI coding assistant? Sorry to be this blunt, but what kind of a stupid question is that?

replies.author: PANC0NE
replies.body:
then what's the point of having any social media or platform when i can simply talk to my ai assistant? :)

i prefer to use it as a tool, and other people's experiences are a better source of learning than "simply talking to my ai"

replies.author: geddy
replies.body: I agree. Plus, it’s better to get some human input, preferably from engineers, about what systems to implement.

replies.author: Optimal-Estimate6576
replies.body:
Ok keep thinking like that... it's your problem not mine anyway.... I couldn't care less. I have launched an online game for android in google play store without the need of any human telling me what to do. Just my AI assistant. My game has supabase, google authentication, billing protocols, transaction security systems, online real time sync services, etc. Asking reddit will likely get you more confused because of divergent opinions. People will advise you according to their subjective experience. 
 It doesn't necessarily mean it's the best option for you. Your AI assistant will probaly find the better solution for you taking into account your limitations and capabilities. One word of advice if you want to actually finish your game: People are unreliable, you need to trust more in yourself and your gut and from my experience you need to have discipline and be persistent. Don't count too much on other people, try to learn by yourself and adopt this rule: if you want something done, do it yourself,  don't wait for others to do it for you.

comments.author: ultra82
comments.body: For a browser game that was built with JS (Three.JS, TS) you can use a simple peer to peer multiplayer architecture, you have WebRTC, you can ask you AI agent to research it and implement it into your game, I did it for a web browser game that I made and it worked just fine.

comments.author: Prestigious_Edge_472
comments.body: Look up nakama, ask your agent if it's suitable for your neeeds, it's open source and can be hosted on a cheap VPS for 5-10 a month. Make sure whatever you do that you communicate to your agent to make everything service agnostic with adapters so you're not stuck in the future if you decide to change the backend. There are managed BaaS but odds are you don't want to pay that much.

replies.author: PANC0NE
replies.body: interesting! i'll keep that in mind, thank you

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
For online multiplayer, you should really start with the multiplayer angle. Adding it after the fact is a lot harder than starting with it. It depends what kind of game you’re making of course that dictates the complexity of adding a multiplayer layer, but essentially the server is what everybody talks to to tell current player positions, then the server re-broadcasts out the position to everybody else. 

I have a multiplayer racing game so I can speak to that end. Each client connects to a server which creates an instance for a race during the race every player constantly sends their “pose”, which is the position of the car. The server then sends every other player that players pose. Then all the players are constantly receiving poses of the other players which the client (in my case it is web-based so the client is a web browser) then renders on screen. 

Net code is a finicky thing because you have to account for things like latency that differs from each client, so the client needs to know how to handle latency. Then there is collision detection which typically happens on the server, because if it happens on my client, everybody has different pings, so you would get a lot of collisions occurring on different clients. The source of truth must be the server so that everybody sees the same race.

That’s just my experience, but that’s a general flow of how online multiplayer works. 

Edit: I forgot to mention this, but another comment did say this, but I’ll say it here as well. The mechanism by which you send and receive data to and from the server is typically a web socket, since it stays open. I use Socket.io for this.

replies.author: PANC0NE
replies.body: thank you! i'll keep this in mind

comments.author: Templeshooter
comments.body:
That depends on what type of game you are making.

The easiest and free-to-start way? Ask your AI agent to use Steam's online services, send a build of your game to your friend and you'll be able to just use Steam's invite or matchmaking.

Same for Epic online services, but I believe you have to create an account and set up stuff first.
